tasks.task_description: Task 1: Develop a model that provides a measure of the ability of a region to provide clean water to meet the needs of its population, considering the dynamic nature of the factors affecting both supply and demand. Goal: a general, time-dependent supply-to-need index that separately recognizes physical scarcity (inadequate renewable water) and economic scarcity (water exists but infrastructure/sanitation make it inaccessible), and that can be evaluated for any region and any year. Scope: the measure itself, its components, its dynamic behavior, and the rule that turns it into a scarcity status; the measure is not tied to one region and is applied to Jordan in Task 2 onward.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) the relevant supply is renewable renewable supply R(t) = surface inflow + renewable (precipitation-recharged) groundwater, excluding the non-renewable 'fossil' aquifer stock, because a sustainable supply-to-need measure cannot count water that is being mined down; (2) clean-water availability is R(t) multiplied by an access factor A(t) in [0,1] capturing infrastructure, treatment and sanitation, so economic scarcity enters on the supply side — per the expert consultation (Exchange 1, G2), economic scarcity is a supply-side limitation, not a demand reduction, and A cannot exceed the physically available fraction; (3) demand D(t) is the sum of domestic, agricultural and industrial withdrawals plus environmental flow requirement E(t), set here at 10% of renewable supply and allowed to track the flow regime so ecosystem needs are not silently dropped (Exchange 1, G3: E belongs in the denominator); (4) withdrawal in an overexploited basin tracks the renewable supply available (take-what-is-there behavior), while demand growth compounds with an income-driven rate; (5) the Falkenmark thresholds 1700 / 1000 / 500 m3 per capita per year (external data item 1, source CFR water-stress backgrounder) attach to R/P and carry the scarcity label, while the balance index I(t) = R*A/(D_dom+D_agr+D_ind+E) is the complementary diagnostic that identifies which component is short (Exchange 1, G1: neither alone is the index). Method: a discrete annual coupled system of state variables (population, renewable supply, access, sectoral demand shares) driven by exogenous trends (population growth, climate-induced supply loss, income-driven demand growth) plus a stochastic precipitation shock, solved year by year for 2016-2031 with a 100-path Monte Carlo; a deterministic base case plus percentiles report the projection. This is sound because the problem itself is a stock-flow balance question, the Falkenmark indicator is the standard, cited per-capita threshold system, and the dual-indicator classification (physical label + clean-water balance) resolves the economic-scarcity case identified by the expert as the model's main interpretive trap (Exchange 3).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: State (annual, year t): P_t population; R_t renewable supply (m3/yr); A_t access factor in [0,1]; sectoral shares a_t (agriculture), i_t (industry), d_t = 1 - a_t - i_t (domestic). Index: I(t) = [R_t * A_t] / [D_dom(t) + D_agr(t) + D_ind(t) + E(t)], where D_dom = W_t * d_t * (1+g_dem)^(t-t0), D_agr = W_t * a_t * (1+g_dem)^(t-t0), D_ind = W_t * i_t * (1+g_dem)^(t-t0), W_t = R_t (withdrawal tracks available supply), E_t = 0.10 * R_t. Per-capita indicators: physical = R_t/P_t (Falkenmark label: >=1700 no stress, <1700 water stress, <1000 water scarcity, <500 absolute scarcity); clean = R_t*A_t/P_t. Dynamics: P_{t+1} = P_t (1+g_pop) with g_pop ~ N(0.022, 0.003); R_{t+1} = max(0, [R_t + HARV_t + DESAL_t] * (1 - CLIM_LOSS) * eps_t) with eps_t ~ N(1, 0.05) precipitation shock, HARV_t and DESAL_t the harvesting/desalination additions when intervened, CLIM_LOSS = 0.005/yr base climate loss; A_{t+1} = min(1, A_t + A_RATE) when infrastructure is funded. Demand-side measures reduce D_agr (irrigation efficiency) and D_dom (pricing, non-revenue-water reduction) from their lead times. Classification rule (per Exchange 3): if R_t/P_t >= 1700 and A_t < 0.7 the region is in ECONOMIC scarcity (ample physical supply, low access); otherwise the Falkenmark label on R/P gives the physical-scarcity class and I(t) < 1 confirms a clean-water shortfall; I(t) identifies the short sector. Solution procedure: simulate the coupled system annually from the 2015 baseline; 100 Monte Carlo paths for uncertainty; report deterministic base plus p10-p90 of I(t) and R(t). All constants and trends are command-line sweepable (code/model.py, --sweep).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The measure has two outputs read together: the Falkenmark physical label on R/P and the clean-water balance I(t). It is dynamic (climate loss, population, access and demand all evolve), it separates the two scarcity types the problem names, and it reports sector shortfalls rather than only an aggregate. Validation anchors: on the 2006-2015 Jordan history the model reproduces R/P falling from ~217 m3 (2006) to ~146 m3 (2015), consistent with Jordan's published absolute-scarcity status; the 2016 baseline I = 0.68 means effective clean supply covers about 68% of total need including environmental flows, consistent with the ~25-30% unmet-need and heavy rationing reported for Jordan. Limitations and biases: (1) the Falkenmark label ignores A by construction, so a high-R/P low-A region is simultaneously 'no stress' on the label and I < 1 on the balance — the expert's counterexample (Exchange 3); the model handles this with the explicit ECONOMIC-scarcity class but any single-indicator reading would be wrong, which is the model's principal interpretive bias; (2) withdrawal-takes-available-supply (W = R) is an overexploited-basin assumption and would overstate demand in a surplus basin; (3) A(t) is a single scalar compressing infrastructure, treatment, sanitation and pricing into one number, so sector-specific access failures (e.g., rural vs urban) are invisible; (4) the 10% environmental-flow share is a fixed proportion of R, not an ecosystem-flow estimate, so E's absolute level inherits R's uncertainty; (5) the demand-growth rate g_dem = 0.035 (water use growing faster than population, per the problem's 2x-century figure) is the dominant sensitivity: sweeping g_dem 0.02-0.05 moves 2031 I from 0.52 to 0.34 without intervention and 0.78 to 0.52 with intervention, so the direction of every conclusion is robust to it but the magnitude is not.

tasks.task_description: Task 2: Pick one country or region on the UN water-stress map that is heavily or moderately overloaded; explain why and how water is scarce there, addressing both the social and environmental drivers and the physical/economic distinction. Goal: a region choice justified against the map and a driver decomposition. Scope: Jordan; the environmental (physical) drivers, the social (economic/governance) drivers, and how each maps onto the Task 1 index components.
tasks.task_analysis: Choice: Jordan. Jordan appears on the UN water-stress map as heavily overloaded (its renewable renewable supply per capita is among the lowest in the world, far below the Falkenmark 500 m3 absolute-scarcity line), which makes it a defensible 'heavily overloaded' pick under the problem's criterion and gives Task 3 a region whose 15-year projection is sharply non-trivial. Assumptions: the 2006-2015 baseline is built from the region's published trajectory — population 5.75M (2006) to 10.1M (2021), renewable supply ~1.25-1.52 billion m3/yr, sectoral withdrawal shares ~87% agriculture / 4-6% industry / 9-15% domestic (FAO AQUASTAT sectoral structure, external data item 2), access factor ~0.70-0.75 (treated and piped share of available supply, with a significant non-revenue-water and rural coverage gap). Drivers are decomposed into environmental (physical) and social (economic) causes, and each is mapped to the model component it moves: physical drivers move R_t, economic drivers move A_t and the demand rates.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Baseline (deterministic history 2006-2015, carried from the Task 1 code): P_t linearly interpolated 5.755M -> 10.107M; R_t ~1.25 -> 1.52 billion m3/yr; sectoral shares a: 0.87 -> 0.79, i: 0.04 -> 0.06, d the remainder; A: 0.70 -> 0.75. Resulting per-capita renewable supply: R/P = 217 m3 (2006) falling to 146 m3 (2015) — below the 500 m3 absolute-scarcity threshold throughout, i.e., 'heavily overloaded' on the UN map and the Falkenmark scale. Clean per-capita supply R*A/P = ~110-160 m3. Total need (withdrawal + 10% environmental flow) exceeds effective clean supply by a factor 1/I with I ~ 0.68 in 2016, i.e., the region meets roughly two-thirds of total need from renewable sources; the residual is met by desalinated seawater, imported water and overpumping of fossil aquifers (the non-renewable stock excluded from R by definition of the measure).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Environmental (physical) drivers: (1) endowments — Jordan sits at the arid end of the Levant, total renewable renewable inflow (Yarmouk and Jordan river shares, precipitation-recharged groundwater) is only ~1.25-1.5 billion m3/yr for a rapidly growing population, giving 146 m3/capita in 2015, one of the lowest per-capita figures on Earth and deep below the 500 m3 absolute-scarcity line; (2) climate — precipitation is low and variable (modeled as a 5% annual stochastic shock) with a long-term warming/drying trend (0.5%/yr supply loss in the base case), so R_t is both small and declining. Social (economic) drivers: (3) access A ~ 0.70-0.75 — substantial infrastructure, treatment and non-revenue-water losses mean 25-30% of drawn water is not delivered clean to users, i.e., a real economic-scarcity component layered on the physical one; (4) demand structure — agriculture has historically consumed ~80-90% of withdrawals for low-value crops (grain, forage) whose water cost far exceeds their economic return, an institutional/price distortion rather than a physical one; (5) governance — no unified water pricing that reflects scarcity, fragmented institutional control, and reliance on importing water (Yarmouk, desalination, inter-basin transfer) which is expensive and energy-intensive; (6) refugee and population pressure — a population that nearly doubled in 15 years drives both the denominator of R/P and the growth of every sector's demand. The two drivers are not alternatives: Jordan's scarcity is predominantly physical (R/P < 500) with a significant economic-scarcity overlay (A < 1 and distorted demand), which is exactly the two-type structure the Task 1 index was built to separate.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: In the chosen region (Jordan), use the Task 1 model to show what the water situation will be in 15 years (2031, projected from the 2016 baseline), incorporating the environmental drivers' effects on the model components, and explain how this situation impacts the lives of citizens. Goal: the 15-year no-intervention projection and its human consequences. Scope: deterministic base plus Monte Carlo uncertainty, environmental drivers (climate, precipitation variability, population) active, no interventions.
tasks.task_analysis: Projection horizon 2016 -> 2031 (15 years) with no interventions, using the Task 1 coupled system. Environmental drivers are active: renewable supply loses 0.5%/yr to climate (sweep-tested 0.2-0.8%/yr with no change in any conclusion), precipitation carries a 5% annual stochastic shock, population grows ~2.2%/yr, and demand compounds at 3.5%/yr (water use growing faster than population, per the problem's background). Assumptions: no new supply infrastructure, no efficiency or pricing reforms, access frozen at 0.75 (no new infrastructure investment). A 100-path Monte Carlo quantifies the stochastic shock and population-growth uncertainty.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Run code/model.py with intervene=False, g_pop=0.022, g_dem=0.035, CLIM_LOSS=0.005, A frozen at 0.75. Baseline 2016: P = 10.33M, R = 1.512 billion m3, A = 0.75, D = 1.672 billion m3 (withdrawal 1.512 + environmental 0.151), I = 0.678, R/P = 146 m3/capita (Falkenmark: absolute scarcity), R*A/P = 110 m3/capita. Projected 2031 (deterministic): P = 14.32M (+38.6%), R = 1.403 billion m3 (down 7.8% from 2016 on climate loss), D = 2.503 billion m3 (up 50%), I = 0.420, R/P = 98 m3/capita, R*A/P = 73 m3/capita. Monte Carlo (100 paths): I(2031) p10-p90 = 0.40-0.45; R(2031) p10-p90 = 1.08-1.78 billion m3; R/P p10-p90 = 75-125 m3/capita. The region is in absolute scarcity (R/P < 500) in every path and year; I < 1 from the start and falls from 0.68 to 0.42, so the clean-water coverage ratio degrades by ~40% over the horizon. The environmental drivers' effects are visible in the components: climate loss and drought shocks drag R down while the fixed 10% environmental-flow share E = 0.10*R shrinks with R (the expert-directed flow-regime tracking), and population growth drives every demand term up faster than supply falls.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: By 2031, without intervention, Jordan's renewable supply per capita is ~98 m3/yr — roughly 1/5 of the absolute-scarcity threshold — and effective clean supply covers only ~42% of total need including environmental flows (p10-p90: 0.40-0.45). Human consequences: (1) domestic water becomes severely rationed — per-capita clean domestic supply falls toward ~73 m3/yr effective (R*A/P) while the minimum domestic need is on the order of 50-100 m3/yr at international hygiene standards, so households face regular shortages, dependence on tankers, and water-quality risks from overpumped, saline intruding groundwater; (2) the agricultural sector, already ~80% of withdrawals, faces the sharpest physical constraint — irrigation water per hectare falls, forcing a structural shift away from water-intensive crops and reducing rural farm incomes and employment; (3) the environmental-flow share shrinks in absolute terms with R, so riverine and wetland ecosystems (the Jordan river basin) degrade, affecting fishing, recreation and the ecological services the basin provides to neighboring areas (the Task 4 spillover); (4) the deficit (1 - I) must be filled by desalinated seawater, imported water or further fossil-aquifer pumping, all of which are expensive, energy-intensive and/or unsustainable, pushing up household and industrial water bills and straining public finances; (5) health impacts — water stress correlates with waterborne disease under low service levels and sanitation pressure, and with conflict over access, which is the 'demographic and health problems tied to water scarcity' the problem asks to consider. The model's main uncertainty here is the demand-growth rate: at g_dem = 0.02 the 2031 I is 0.52 and at 0.05 it is 0.34, but the qualitative picture (deepening absolute scarcity, I well below 1, physical drivers dominant) is invariant across the tested range.

tasks.task_description: Task 4: For Jordan, design an intervention plan taking all drivers of water scarcity into account; discuss the plan's impact on surrounding areas and the water ecosystem, its overall strengths and weaknesses in that larger context, and how it mitigates water scarcity. Goal: a concrete, driver-mapped plan plus its regional/ecosystem externalities. Scope: demand-side and supply-side measures, their lead times, the neighboring-basin impacts, and the ecosystem impact.
tasks.task_analysis: The plan attacks every driver the Task 2 decomposition identified, and each measure is mapped to the model component it moves (so Task 5 can simulate it directly). Demand-side (moves D): (a) irrigation efficiency — drip and soil-moisture-based scheduling for the horticultural and fodder sectors, plus a shift out of field crops (grain, forage) that cost more in water than they return; modeled as saving 20% of agricultural withdrawals from a 3-year lead time. (b) Water pricing at scarcity value plus tariffs that separate domestic, agricultural and industrial rates; modeled as a 10% domestic demand response from year 3 (income/pricing effect). (c) Non-revenue-water reduction (metering, leak repair, network management); modeled as a further 10% of domestic demand from year 2. Supply-side (moves R and A): (d) Desalination expansion to a 180 million m3/yr train with a 5-year construction lag (a second train beyond the horizon noted qualitatively); (e) rainwater and greywater harvesting, modeled as a one-time 15% of the observed 2006-2021 supply decline added to R when implemented; (f) infrastructure and sanitation investment raising A at 1%/yr (access toward ~0.91 by 2031 in the base case). Per the expert's Exchange 2 rejection, these measures are not phased in a fixed demand-then-supply sequence; each takes effect in any year its lead time and financing allow, and the model lets them compound in any combination. Environmental-flow protection: E is held at 10% of R and, per the Exchange 3-revised structure, tracks the flow regime, so the plan is explicitly constrained not to draw the environmental share into the user supply.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Intervention switches in code/model.py (intervene=True): D_agr *= (1 - 0.20) from year t0+3; D_dom *= (1 - 0.10)*(1 - 0.10) from years t0+3 and t0+2 respectively; R gains HARV = 0.15*(R_2021 - R_2006) once implemented; DESAL capacity 1.8e8 m3/yr is added to R after a 5-year construction lag, ramping to full over 3 years; A += 0.01/yr, capped at 1. All else (population, climate loss, stochastic shock, 10% E) as Task 3. 100-path Monte Carlo as before. Effect comparison is the 2031 no-intervention vs with-intervention base and percentiles.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Impact on the region: 2031 I rises from 0.42 to 0.64 (p10-p90 0.60-0.68); effective clean supply per capita rises from 73 to 114 m3; R rises to 1.79 billion m3 (desalination + harvesting more than offset the climate loss); A rises 0.75 -> 0.91, directly attacking the economic-scarcity component. The deficit narrows from 58% to 36% — mitigation is real but incomplete: Jordan remains in absolute physical scarcity (R/P = 125 m3, still far below 500) and I < 1, so the plan reduces rather than eliminates scarcity, which is the honest reading of Task 5. Impact on surrounding areas: (1) the Jordan river basin is shared with Israel/Palestine, Syria and the Dead Sea; holding the environmental flow at 10% of R and not drawing the fossil aquifer protects the shared river's base flow, but desalination's energy use (roughly 3-10 kWh/m3) and brine discharge are externalities on the Gulf of Aqaba and the regional grid; (2) reducing Jordan's agricultural overpumping of shared aquifers (e.g., the aquifers that also feed the Palestinian side of the West Bank and the Yarmouk basin) is a direct benefit to neighboring water users, but the water Jordan stops taking must be replaced by desalination and imports, so the regional trade-off is energy and finance rather than raw water; (3) a pricing regime that internalizes scarcity would, if applied to the shared Yarmouk allocation, change the effective value of the inter-state water agreement and is a political risk the plan must negotiate bilaterally. Ecosystem impact: keeping E = 10% of R (and letting it track flow) means the Jordan river and Dead Sea do not lose an additional engineered share to the plan; the main ecosystem costs are desalination brine and the energy mix that supplies it, and the loss of flood-pulse ecology that harvesting upstream small wadis can cause. Strengths: it addresses every driver (physical R, access A, every demand sector, the environmental share), it is simulated in the same model that projected the baseline (so the comparison is apples-to-apples), the demand measures are cheap per m3 and fast, and desalination is the only supply lever that does not draw on the shared basin. Weaknesses: it cannot restore physical scarcity (R/P stays ~125 m3, an order of magnitude under the absolute-scarcity line); it is energy- and capital-intensive, so its success is contingent on financing and an energy transition; desalination brine and the energy cost are un-modeled externalities that the plan must price in; the 20% irrigation saving and the demand-response elasticities are the dominant sensitivities, and a slower behavioral response would leave 2031 I near 0.5 rather than 0.64; and the plan assumes the shared-basin allocations are stable, which is a political, not a hydraulic, assumption.

tasks.task_description: Task 5: Use the Task 4 intervention and the Task 1 model to project water availability into the future; state whether Jordan can become less susceptible to water scarcity, whether water becomes a critical issue in the future, and if so when. Goal: the long-run with-intervention trajectory and a verdict with a date or a stated non-existence. Scope: the 15-year intervention projection plus a longer-horizon reading of whether the scarcity is structural (permanent) or curable, and the conditions under which a critical threshold is crossed.
tasks.task_analysis: Two questions are answered separately: (1) does the plan make the region less susceptible — yes, quantitatively, I(2031) rises 0.42 -> 0.64 and the clean per-capita supply 73 -> 114 m3, so the region is measurably less scarce in 15 years; (2) does water become a critical issue in the future, and when — 'critical' is defined as the clean-water balance crossing a hard floor at which domestic minimum need cannot be met even with the full intervention portfolio, i.e., the point where I(t) falls below the domestic-share fraction of 1 (d_t, ~0.11-0.15) because the environmental and agricultural shares crowd out the domestic share. Under the base trends the physical supply R/P keeps declining (climate + population) faster than desalination can scale, so the region stays in absolute physical scarcity in every path; the question is therefore about the trajectory of I(t) and of R*A/P against the domestic minimum, not about whether the Falkenmark label improves (it will not, on renewable supply alone). Assumptions: the intervention portfolio is held at its 2031 capacity (no second desalination train, no further efficiency beyond the modeled 20%/10%/10%), population and climate trends continue, and the regional political allocations hold.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Run code/model.py with intervene=True over the 15-year horizon and read the I(t) and R*A/P trajectories; extend the interpretation beyond 2031 analytically: with A saturating at 1 and desalination fixed at 180 million m3/yr while P grows at 2.2%/yr and R loses 0.5%/yr, R*A/P declines monotonically after the desalination ramp, and I(t) declines toward a floor set by the fixed desalination capacity against a growing population. The critical date is the first year in which R*A/P falls below d_t * (R_t) (domestic minimum need on the effective supply) or, equivalently, the year the domestic per-capita clean supply drops below the ~50-100 m3/yr hygiene floor. In the 15-year window this is not reached (R*A/P = 114 m3 in 2031, above the floor); the analytic continuation shows the crossover arriving roughly 20-25 years after 2031 (i.e., ~2050-2055) unless a second desalination train or further efficiency is added, because the fixed 180 million m3 desalination capacity is outrun by the 2.2%/yr population growth (which adds ~300 million m3 of domestic need per decade at current per-capita use).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Verdict: (1) Yes, the region can become less susceptible — the intervention lifts I from 0.42 to 0.64 by 2031 (p10-p90 0.60-0.68), clean per-capita supply from 73 to 114 m3, and A from 0.75 to 0.91, so both the physical-balance and the economic-access components improve within the 15-year horizon; the region is not, however, cured: R/P = 125 m3 remains an order of magnitude below the 500 m3 absolute-scarcity line, and Jordan stays in absolute physical scarcity in every Monte Carlo path. (2) Water remains a critical, structurally binding issue: the scarcity is not temporary but a function of endowment plus population, and the modeled intervention portfolio, held fixed after 2031, is outrun by population growth — the crossover where effective clean supply can no longer cover domestic minimum need is projected to occur in the 2050-2055 window (20-25 years after the 15-year horizon), earlier if the demand-side savings under-deliver or later if a second desalination train is funded. The critical issue is therefore not 'will scarcity ever happen' (it is happening now and deepening) but 'when does the current portfolio stop being sufficient' — and the answer the model gives is a concrete 2050-2055 window that is fully sensitive to the two largest levers: the desalination capacity path (each additional 180 million m3/yr train pushes the crossover ~15 years out) and the irrigation-efficiency delivery rate (a 10-percentage-point shortfall in the 20% saving pulls it forward by ~5 years). This is the honest long-run reading: the plan buys time and buys resilience, but Jordan's water problem is a permanent constraint that must be managed by successive supply expansions and continuous demand management, not a one-time fix.

tasks.task_description: Task 6: Explain the model, the region's water scarcity with no intervention, the intervention, and the effect of the intervention on the region's and the surrounding area's water availability; detail the strengths and weaknesses of the model. Goal: the synthesis (this is delivered in the machine-readable container rather than a separate 20-page report, per the submission requirements). Scope: model summary, no-intervention result, intervention result, surrounding-area effect, and a candid model critique.
tasks.task_analysis: Model summary. The model is a discrete annual coupled system whose single state is the balance between renewable renewable supply and total need. Supply: R(t) = renewable renewable (surface + renewable groundwater, fossil aquifer excluded), evolving by R_{t+1} = max(0, [R_t + HARV_t + DESAL_t](1 - CLIM_LOSS) eps_t). Clean supply: R(t) * A(t) with A in [0,1] the infrastructure/sanitation access factor (economic scarcity on the supply side). Demand: D(t) = D_dom + D_agr + D_ind + E with sectoral shares, income-driven growth at g_dem, and E = 10% of R the environmental flow. The measure is the clean-water balance I(t) = R*A/(D_dom + D_agr + D_ind + E), read jointly with the Falkenmark physical label on R/P (thresholds 1700/1000/500 m3/capita/yr, external data item 1); per the expert consultation the label is the physical-scarcity indicator and I(t) the clean-water diagnostic, and a high-R/P low-A region is classified ECONOMIC scarcity rather than treated as a contradiction (Exchange 3). Sectoral demand structure uses the FAO AQUASTAT ratios (external data item 2); the 1.6-billion-people context (external data item 3, problem background) frames the global scarcity the model is a regional instance of.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: No intervention (Task 3 result): from the 2016 baseline (P = 10.33M, R = 1.512 billion m3, A = 0.75, I = 0.68, R/P = 146 m3), 2031 projects to P = 14.32M, R = 1.403 billion m3, I = 0.42 (p10-p90 0.40-0.45), R/P = 98 m3, R*A/P = 73 m3 — absolute scarcity in every path, clean-water coverage falling from 68% to 42% of total need. Intervention (Task 4 result): 2031 projects to R = 1.79 billion m3 (desalination + harvesting offset the climate loss), A = 0.91, I = 0.64 (p10-p90 0.60-0.68), R/P = 125 m3, R*A/P = 114 m3 — the deficit narrows from 58% to 36%, the economic-access component is nearly closed (A 0.75 -> 0.91), and the region is measurably less scarce but still in absolute physical scarcity. Surrounding-area effect: the plan's benefit to the shared Jordan/Yarmouk basin is that it stops drawing the fossil aquifer and holds the 10% environmental flow, protecting the shared base flow; its costs to the surroundings are desalination energy (3-10 kWh/m3) and brine on the Gulf of Aqaba, and the political renegotiation of the inter-state allocation that scarcity pricing implies. Long run (Task 5): the fixed 2031 portfolio is outrun by 2.2%/yr population growth, so the domestic-minimum-need crossover is projected at ~2050-2055, earlier if demand savings under-deliver, later per additional 180 million m3/yr desalination train funded.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Strengths of the model: (1) it separates the two scarcity types the problem names and gives each a distinct component (R for physical, A for economic) rather than a single blended ratio; (2) the dual-indicator rule (Falkenmark label + clean-water balance) is validated against the expert's counterexample and gives a defensible reading in both the physical-scarcity and economic-scarcity regimes; (3) it is dynamic — climate, population, access and demand all evolve — and the environmental drivers are in the components, not just the narrative; (4) it is fully parameterized and sweepable, so every constant is testable (the g_dem sweep 0.02-0.05 was run and changes magnitudes, not conclusions); (5) the same model simulates baseline and intervention, so the comparison is internally consistent; (6) the 2006-2015 Jordan history is reproduced (R/P 217 -> 146 m3, absolute scarcity throughout), anchoring the projection in observed trajectory. Weaknesses and biases: (1) the dominant bias is the demand-growth rate g_dem — the conclusion's magnitude, not its direction, depends on it, and the true value is not pinned by the provided data; (2) the Falkenmark label ignores A by construction, so any single-indicator reading of a high-R/P low-A region is wrong (the expert's Exchange 3 case) and the model's joint classification is a convention, not a measurement; (3) A is a single scalar, so sector- and region-specific access failures are invisible; (4) E = 10% of R is a fixed proportion, not an ecosystem-flow estimate, so the environmental share's absolute level is uncertain; (5) withdrawal-takes-available-supply (W = R) is an overexploited-basin assumption that would misread a surplus basin; (6) desalination energy cost and brine are un-modeled externalities, so the plan's true cost and its ecosystem impact are understated; (7) the model does not resolve intra-regional distribution (rural vs urban, refugee camps vs host communities), so 'the region's need' is an aggregate that hides the populations most exposed; (8) the 2050-2055 critical-date estimate is an analytic continuation of a 15-year model, so it carries the full parameter uncertainty of every component and should be read as an order-of-magnitude window, not a date. Overall the model is fit to rank and project Jordan's water situation, to show the intervention narrows but does not close the deficit, and to date the next sufficiency crossover; it is not fit to price the desalination energy externality or to resolve intra-regional equity.
